title: Metformin and Alcohol: Low Blood Sugar, Lactic Acidosis, and PCOS
excerpt: Can you drink alcohol on metformin? How the two interact in your liver, the real risks of low blood sugar and lactic acidosis, what changes if you take it for PCOS, and the warning signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on metformin? How alcohol and metformin interact, low blood sugar and lactic acidosis risks, PCOS use, and when to call a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most people who take metformin can have an occasional drink, and many doctors are fine with light, moderate drinking alongside it. The two real risks are **low blood sugar** (hypoglycemia), which is more likely if you drink on an empty stomach or also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, and **lactic acidosis**, a rare but dangerous build-up of acid in the blood that heavy or binge drinking makes more likely. Metformin's own US label specifically warns against "excessive alcohol intake." So the line isn't between zero drinks and one drink. It's between a glass of wine with dinner and a night of heavy drinking.

**The quick rules:** Drink with food, never on an empty stomach. Keep it to light or moderate amounts, and avoid binges. If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea (such as glipizide, glyburide, or glimepiride) along with metformin, check your blood sugar before bed and have a snack. Don't stop or skip metformin on your own to "make room" for drinking. If you're vomiting or badly dehydrated after a night out, call your doctor or pharmacist about whether to pause your dose, because dehydration is one of the things that raises lactic acidosis risk.

> **This is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about alcohol and your metformin.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for someone who knows your kidney function, your other medicines, and why you take metformin. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you or someone who takes metformin has trouble breathing or very fast breathing, unusual muscle pain, severe stomach pain with vomiting, a slow or irregular heartbeat, feels unusually cold or weak, or is confused or very hard to wake after drinking. Those can be signs of lactic acidosis or severe low blood sugar, and both need treatment fast. **Check with your doctor before drinking at all if** you have kidney disease, liver disease, heart failure, a history of pancreatitis, or you drink heavily most days.

## How Metformin and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Metformin is the most widely prescribed first-line medicine for type 2 diabetes. It's sold as Glucophage, Glumetza, Fortamet, Riomet, and in many generics, and it's also in combination pills such as Janumet (with sitagliptin) and Synjardy (with empagliflozin). It's also commonly prescribed off-label for PCOS and prediabetes.

To understand why alcohol matters, it helps to know what metformin does. Its main job is to **reduce how much sugar your liver releases into your blood**. Your liver constantly makes new glucose (a process called gluconeogenesis, which just means "making new sugar") to keep your blood sugar steady between meals and overnight. Metformin turns that process down. It also helps your muscles respond better to insulin.

Alcohol happens to act on the same organ, and in some of the same ways. That overlap is where both risks come from.

### Risk 1: Alcohol and metformin both push blood sugar down

When your liver is breaking down alcohol, it puts that job first. Processing alcohol uses up a helper molecule (NAD+) that the liver also needs to make new glucose. So while alcohol is in your system, your liver's ability to make sugar drops, sometimes sharply.

Now stack that on top of metformin, which is already turning down the liver's sugar output. On a normal day, you're fine, because food keeps your blood sugar up. But if you drink without eating, or drink heavily, or go to bed after drinking without a snack, your liver has less ability to rescue you if your blood sugar falls.

Metformin on its own rarely causes low blood sugar. That's one of the reasons doctors like it. The low-blood-sugar risk with alcohol goes up a lot when:

- You drink on an empty stomach or skip meals
- You drink heavily or binge
- You also take **insulin** or a **sulfonylurea** (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride), which push blood sugar down much harder than metformin does
- You exercise hard (dancing counts) while drinking
- You're asleep and not eating for many hours after drinking

### Risk 2: Alcohol raises lactic acid, and so can metformin

Lactic acid is a normal by-product your body makes all the time, especially in muscles. Your liver is the main organ that clears it, partly by turning it back into glucose.

Metformin slightly reduces how well the liver clears lactate. In healthy kidneys and a healthy liver, that's almost never a problem. Alcohol does something similar: while the liver is busy processing alcohol, it clears lactate less efficiently, and lactate levels can rise.

Put the two together in large amounts, and lactate can build up faster than your body removes it. That's **lactic acidosis**. It's rare, but when it happens it's a medical emergency and can be fatal. The US prescribing information for metformin carries a **boxed warning** (the FDA's strongest kind) about lactic acidosis, and it lists excessive alcohol intake among the risk factors. The label states that alcohol potentiates metformin's effect on lactate metabolism and tells prescribers to warn patients against excessive alcohol intake, whether in a single binge or over time.

The other major risk factors on that label matter too, because several of them overlap with heavy drinking:

- Poor kidney function (metformin is cleared by the kidneys, so it can build up)
- Liver problems
- Dehydration, which is common after a night of drinking, especially with vomiting or diarrhea
- Serious illness, surgery, or infection
- Heart failure or low oxygen levels
- Being older, typically 65 and over

This is why "a glass of wine with dinner" and "a heavy night out followed by a day of vomiting" are completely different situations for someone on metformin.

## What the Research and Official Guidance Actually Say

**Lactic acidosis is rare.** Large reviews of metformin use, including a well-known Cochrane review, have found that serious lactic acidosis is uncommon in people taking metformin who don't have major risk factors. Most reported cases involve other problems at the same time, such as kidney failure, severe infection, or heavy alcohol use. The rarity is real, but so is the severity, which is why the warning exists.

**The label draws the line at excessive drinking, not all drinking.** The FDA-approved labeling doesn't tell patients to avoid alcohol entirely. It warns against excessive intake. That's consistent with how most diabetes care teams approach it.

**Diabetes organizations allow moderate drinking for many people.** The American Diabetes Association's guidance says adults with diabetes who choose to drink should do so in moderation (no more than one drink a day for women and two for men), and should be aware of the risk of delayed low blood sugar, especially if they use insulin or insulin-releasing medicines. The ADA also advises drinking with food and checking blood sugar.

**Low blood sugar from alcohol can be delayed.** Doctors have long noted that alcohol-related hypoglycemia can show up hours after drinking, including overnight and into the next morning. That's the main reason for the "check before bed and eat a snack" advice.

Put simply: the research and official guidance say moderate drinking is usually acceptable for people on metformin with healthy kidneys and liver, while heavy drinking, binges, and drinking while dehydrated or sick are what raise the serious risks.

## How Much Alcohol Is Safe on Metformin?

There's no single safe number for everyone, and your doctor's answer should outrank any general figure. But here is how the general guidance lines up:

| Situation | General guidance |
|---|---|
| Healthy kidneys and liver, metformin only | Many doctors are comfortable with moderate drinking: up to 1 drink a day for women and 2 for men, with food. |
| Also taking insulin or a sulfonylurea | Same limits at most, plus checking blood sugar before bed and eating a carb-containing snack. Ask your doctor for specific advice. |
| Kidney disease, liver disease, or heart failure | Ask your doctor before drinking at all. These conditions raise lactic acidosis risk on their own. |
| Binge drinking (4+ drinks for women, 5+ for men in a few hours) | This is the "excessive intake" the label warns about. Avoid it on metformin. |
| Heavy drinking most days | Talk to your doctor. Regular heavy drinking raises lactic acidosis risk and can damage the liver over time. |

A "standard drink" in the US is about 14 grams of pure alcohol: roughly 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof spirits. A large restaurant pour of wine or a strong craft beer can easily be closer to two.

### What you drink matters, not just how much

Different drinks affect blood sugar differently, and that can confuse people who check their glucose.

- **Beer, sweet wine, cider, and mixed drinks with juice or regular soda** contain carbohydrates. They can push blood sugar *up* at first, then the alcohol can pull it *down* hours later. The early rise can give false reassurance.
- **Dry wine and spirits with zero-calorie mixers** have little or no sugar, so there's no early rise. The later drop from the alcohol can still happen.
- **Shots and strong cocktails** get a lot of alcohol in quickly, which is the pattern most linked to both risks.

No drink type is automatically safe. The amount and whether you've eaten matter more.

## Low Blood Sugar After Drinking: What to Watch For

The tricky part is that low blood sugar can look a lot like being drunk. Both can cause:

- Dizziness or unsteadiness
- Confusion or slurred speech
- Sleepiness
- Irritability or acting strangely
- Blurred vision

Signs that point more toward low blood sugar include **shakiness, sweating, a pounding heart, sudden hunger, and pale or clammy skin**. But when you've been drinking, you can't reliably tell the difference by how you feel, and neither can the people around you. That's why checking with a meter or continuous glucose monitor (CGM) is the only way to know.

### How to handle it

If you check and your blood sugar is low (generally under 70 mg/dL), the standard approach many diabetes educators teach is the "rule of 15": take about 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, such as glucose tablets, 4 ounces of juice, or regular (non-diet) soda, wait 15 minutes, and recheck. Repeat if you're still low, then eat a snack or meal once you're back up. Your own care team may give you different targets, so follow theirs.

A few alcohol-specific points:

- **Glucagon may work less well after heavy drinking.** Emergency glucagon works by making the liver release stored sugar. Heavy drinking can use up those stores, so glucagon may be less effective. That's another reason to prevent lows rather than rely on treating them.
- **Tell the people you're with.** If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, make sure someone knows you have diabetes and what a low looks like. A medical ID bracelet or phone medical ID helps first responders who might otherwise assume you're just drunk.
- **Anyone who can't swallow safely or won't wake up needs emergency care.** Don't put food or drink in the mouth of someone who isn't fully awake. Call 911.

For a deeper look at drinking with diabetes in general, including meal planning and glucose targets, see our [alcohol and diabetes blood sugar management guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

## Lactic Acidosis: The Rare Risk You Should Know By Name

Most people on metformin will never come near lactic acidosis. But because it's serious and the early signs are vague, it's worth knowing what it looks like, especially after a heavy night.

**Symptoms of lactic acidosis can include:**

- Unusual muscle pain or cramping that isn't from exercise
- Trouble breathing or fast, deep breathing
- Unusual sleepiness, weakness, or feeling very tired
- Stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting
- Feeling cold, especially in the hands and feet
- Dizziness or lightheadedness
- A slow or irregular heartbeat

Notice how much of that overlaps with a bad hangover. That's the danger. Someone who takes metformin, drank heavily, then spent the next day vomiting and unable to keep fluids down could have both a hangover and the early stages of a real problem. Vomiting and diarrhea cause dehydration, and dehydration can affect the kidneys, which then clear metformin less well.

**Get emergency care if** someone on metformin has fast or labored breathing, severe weakness, confusion, or symptoms that feel much worse than a normal hangover, or that are getting worse instead of better. Tell the medical team they take metformin. Lactic acidosis is diagnosed with a blood test and treated in the hospital.

## The Morning After: Metformin and Hangovers

Even when nothing dangerous happens, metformin and alcohol can make each other's side effects worse the next day.

**Stomach trouble.** Metformin's most common side effects are digestive: nausea, diarrhea, gas, bloating, and stomach upset. Alcohol irritates the gut lining and speeds things through. Together they can make a hangover noticeably rougher. If this is a regular pattern for you, our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains what's going on and what helps.

**Dehydration.** Alcohol makes you pee more, and diarrhea or vomiting adds to the fluid loss. For most people this is just part of a hangover. On metformin, it matters a bit more, because dehydration is one of the conditions that can push lactic acidosis risk up.

**Should you take your morning metformin when hungover?** If you feel normal-ish, can eat, and can keep fluids down, most people simply take their usual dose with breakfast. If you're vomiting, can't keep food or water down, or are badly dehydrated, that's when to call your doctor or pharmacist. Several health services teach "sick day rules" for diabetes, where some medicines including metformin are paused temporarily during dehydrating illnesses. Whether that applies to you, and for how long, is a question for your care team, not something to decide on your own the first time it comes up. Ask about it at your next appointment so you have a plan in advance.

**Taking pain relievers with a hangover.** If you reach for something for a headache, the usual cautions apply. Acetaminophen and alcohol have their own liver concerns, covered in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). NSAIDs like ibuprofen can be hard on the kidneys when you're dehydrated, which matters more for people on metformin. See our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) for details, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure which is better for you.

## Metformin and Alcohol for PCOS

A lot of people searching "metformin and alcohol" don't have diabetes at all. Metformin is widely prescribed off-label for **polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)**, where it can help with insulin resistance, cycle regularity, and sometimes weight. People with PCOS on metformin are often younger and more likely to be drinking socially, so the question comes up a lot.

The same basic mechanism applies, with a few differences:

- **Low blood sugar risk is generally lower** if you don't have diabetes and you're on metformin alone, because your body's own blood sugar control is still working. But it isn't zero. Drinking heavily on an empty stomach, especially if you're also dieting or exercising hard, can still lead to a low.
- **Lactic acidosis risk depends on the same factors**: kidney function, dehydration, and heavy or binge drinking. Being young and healthy lowers your baseline risk, but binges are still the pattern to avoid.
- **The stomach side effects are often worse early on.** Many people with PCOS start metformin and spend the first weeks dealing with nausea and diarrhea. Adding alcohol during that adjustment period tends to make it worse. Some people find the extended-release (ER or XR) version easier on the stomach. That's a question for your prescriber.
- **Alcohol can work against some of the reasons you're taking metformin.** Alcohol adds calories, can increase appetite, and heavy drinking can affect hormone balance and insulin sensitivity. If weight or cycle regularity is one of your goals, frequent drinking pulls in the opposite direction.

If you have PCOS and take metformin, the practical advice is the same: eat when you drink, keep it moderate, avoid binges, hydrate, and talk with your prescriber about what's reasonable for you.

## Metformin for Weight Loss or Prediabetes

Metformin is also prescribed for prediabetes, and sometimes off-label to help with weight. If that's you, the safety picture is similar to the PCOS case: lower hypoglycemia risk than someone with diabetes on several medicines, the same lactic acidosis warning around heavy drinking, and the same tendency for alcohol to undercut the goal. Calories from drinks add up quickly. Our guide on [alcohol and weight loss](/never-hungover/alcohol-weight-loss-metabolic-guide-2025) covers how drinking affects metabolism and fat storage.

If you're on a GLP-1 medicine such as Ozempic or Mounjaro alongside metformin, which is a common combination, there are extra things to know about how those drugs change alcohol cravings and stomach symptoms. See our [Ozempic, GLP-1, and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ozempic-glp1-alcohol-hangover-2026-research-guide).

## Timing: How Long After Metformin Can You Drink?

This is a very common question, and the honest answer is that **timing doesn't really work as a safety strategy with metformin.**

Metformin is a daily maintenance medicine. Once you've been taking it regularly, it doesn't drop to zero between doses in a way that creates a "safe window." Spacing your drink a few hours away from your pill doesn't meaningfully change the interaction. What changes the risk is **how much you drink, whether you've eaten, how hydrated you are, and your kidney and liver health.**

That also means:

- **Don't skip a dose to drink.** Skipping metformin doesn't make heavy drinking safe, and it disrupts your blood sugar control. If you think you need to adjust your dose around drinking, that's a conversation for your doctor.
- **Don't double up the next day** if you missed a dose. Follow your prescription's missed-dose instructions.
- **Extended-release metformin** is usually taken once a day with the evening meal. If that's when you tend to drink, the most important thing is the same as always: eat the meal, keep the drinks moderate.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from mixing metformin and alcohol if you:

- Have **reduced kidney function** (your doctor tracks this with a blood test called eGFR)
- Have **liver disease**, including fatty liver disease or hepatitis
- Have **heart failure** or a lung condition that lowers your oxygen levels
- Also take **insulin or a sulfonylurea**
- Are **65 or older**
- Tend to **binge drink** or drink heavily most days
- Often drink **without eating**, or follow a very low-calorie or fasting diet
- Have had **pancreatitis** before

If any of these describe you, have a short conversation with your doctor or pharmacist about what's safe. They can look at your lab results and full medication list. For a broader overview of how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## A Practical Plan for a Night Out on Metformin

If your doctor is fine with you drinking moderately, these habits cover most of the risk:

1. **Eat a real meal** before or while you drink, with some carbohydrate and protein.
2. **Set a limit before you start**, and count drinks honestly. Large pours count as more than one.
3. **Alternate with water** to slow down and stay hydrated.
4. **Pick lower-sugar options** if you're watching glucose, but don't assume they're "safe" in larger amounts.
5. **If you use insulin or a sulfonylurea, check your blood sugar** before bed and eat a snack with carbs if it's on the low side or you're unsure. A CGM with alarms is helpful here.
6. **Tell a friend** you have diabetes and what a low looks like, if that applies to you.
7. **Take your normal morning metformin with breakfast** if you're well. If you're vomiting or can't keep fluids down, call your doctor or pharmacist.

## Where Supplements Like DHM Fit In

If you're on metformin and you drink, the biggest wins come from the habits above, not from any supplement. Still, people often ask whether a hangover supplement is a reasonable addition. Here's an honest view:

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies. A small 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease reported improvements in some liver and metabolic markers, and some animal research has looked at DHM's effects on blood sugar. That last point is a reason for caution rather than excitement: if a supplement might nudge blood sugar, you want your doctor to know about it when you're already on a glucose-lowering medicine.
- **There is no good evidence that DHM lowers the risk of lactic acidosis or low blood sugar from alcohol**, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe on metformin.
- If your doctor is comfortable with it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

For the habits that make the most difference to how you feel the next day, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through what the evidence supports.

## The Bottom Line

- Most people on metformin can drink moderately, with food, if their doctor agrees.
- The two real risks are **low blood sugar**, which is more likely on an empty stomach or with insulin or sulfonylureas, and **lactic acidosis**, which is rare but serious and linked to heavy drinking, dehydration, and kidney or liver problems.
- Metformin's own label warns against excessive alcohol intake. Binges are the pattern to avoid.
- Low blood sugar can look like being drunk. If you use insulin or a sulfonylurea, check your glucose before bed and eat a snack.
- Timing your drinks around your pill doesn't make heavy drinking safer. Don't skip doses on your own.
- If you're vomiting and dehydrated after drinking, call your doctor about your metformin. If someone on metformin has trouble breathing, severe weakness, or confusion, get emergency care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking metformin?**

Many people can, in moderation and with food, if their doctor agrees. Metformin's label warns against excessive alcohol intake because it raises the risk of lactic acidosis, and drinking on an empty stomach can contribute to low blood sugar. If you have kidney disease, liver disease, heart failure, or take insulin or a sulfonylurea, ask your doctor before drinking.

**What happens if you drink alcohol on metformin?**

With a drink or two and a meal, usually nothing noticeable for most people. Heavier drinking can lower blood sugar, because alcohol stops the liver from releasing sugar while metformin already reduces that output. It can also raise lactic acid levels. Rarely, especially with binge drinking, dehydration, or kidney problems, this leads to lactic acidosis, a medical emergency. Stomach side effects like nausea and diarrhea also tend to get worse.

**How long after taking metformin can I drink alcohol?**

There isn't a meaningful safe waiting window. Metformin is a daily medicine that stays in your system with regular use, so spacing a drink a few hours from your pill doesn't change the interaction much. What matters is how much you drink, whether you've eaten, and how hydrated you are. Don't skip doses to drink without talking to your doctor.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking metformin for PCOS?**

Generally, moderate drinking with food is considered reasonable for many people taking metformin for PCOS, but check with your prescriber. Low blood sugar is less likely if you don't have diabetes, though heavy drinking on an empty stomach can still cause it. Binge drinking still raises lactic acidosis risk, and alcohol often makes metformin's stomach side effects worse, especially in the first few weeks.

**What are the signs of lactic acidosis from metformin and alcohol?**

Signs include unusual muscle pain, trouble breathing or fast breathing, unusual sleepiness or weakness, stomach pain with nausea or vomiting, feeling cold, dizziness, and a slow or irregular heartbeat. Many of these overlap with a bad hangover, so if symptoms are severe, getting worse, or include breathing trouble or confusion, get emergency care and tell the medical team you take metformin.

**Does alcohol cause low blood sugar on metformin?**

It can. Metformin alone rarely causes low blood sugar, but alcohol temporarily blocks the liver from making new glucose, and metformin already turns that output down. The risk is highest when you drink without eating, drink heavily, or also take insulin or a sulfonylurea. Lows can be delayed, sometimes overnight, so checking your blood sugar before bed and eating a snack helps.

**Should I skip my metformin if I'm going to drink?**

Don't skip or change your dose on your own. Skipping metformin doesn't make heavy drinking safe and can disrupt your blood sugar control. If you're vomiting or badly dehydrated after drinking, call your doctor or pharmacist, because some care teams advise pausing metformin during dehydrating illness. Ask about a plan for that ahead of time.

**Is DHM safe to take with metformin?**

There isn't good human research on combining DHM with metformin, and some animal studies suggest DHM may affect blood sugar, so ask your doctor before adding it. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers the risk of lactic acidosis or low blood sugar from alcohol, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe on metformin.
